carb-040.title: Arrow Canyon marks the Pennsylvanian
carb-040.text: In Arrow Canyon, Nevada, a single layer of rock marks the start of the Pennsylvanian and its first stage, the Bashkirian. The boundary is set by the first appearance of a conodont, Declinognathodus noduliferus.

carb-050.title: The first great glacial maximum
carb-050.text: In North America, a gap in the rocks separates the Mississippian from the Pennsylvanian. That unconformity is the scar of a falling sea. The ice age's first major glacial period, from the Serpukhovian to the Moscovian, spread ice sheets from cores in southern Africa and South America. In the Bashkirian, a global sea-level fall marked its first major glacial maximum. At the boundary, a positive oxygen-isotope excursion, a chemical sign of growing ice, matches sea-level falls and glacial deposits across southern Gondwana. Early in the Bashkirian, the ocean gateway between the Rheic and the Tethys closed. That changed ocean circulation and added to the cooling.

carb-038.title: All modern classes of fungi appear
carb-038.text: By the late Carboniferous, every modern class of fungi had appeared. Rocks of Pennsylvanian age preserve them, showing that the fungal world of today was already fully sketched out among the coal swamps.

carb-039.title: Oxygen reaches its all-time high
carb-039.text:
Today the air is 21% oxygen. In the Pennsylvanian it reached 25 to 30%. All models agree on the rise, from 15–20% at the start of the Carboniferous to those highs.

Pyrite, an iron sulfide mineral, gives a more detailed record. It suggests about 15% early in the period, over 25% in the Pennsylvanian, then a drop below 20% toward its end. Charcoal tells the same story. Remains of wildfires grow more common from the Late Devonian into the Carboniferous, because fire burns more readily in richer air.

The source of the extra oxygen was the coal forests. Their photosynthesis released oxygen into the air, and their buried peat kept the carbon from taking it back by decay, as {{ref:carb-044}} describes. Whether the oxygen-rich air let arthropods and other animals grow large is still debated.

carb-041.title: Carbon dioxide falls to an all-time low
carb-041.text: Carbon dioxide in the air fell below 300 ppm in the Pennsylvanian and early Permian, one of its lowest levels ever. Several processes pulled it down: burial of organic matter, widespread ocean anoxia, and weathering of the rising Central Pangean Mountains. Fast-growing coal forests locked away more carbon, and a very late Carboniferous forest resurgence brought polar ice back to Gondwana. Near the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, erosion of dark, iron-rich mountain rocks pushed carbon dioxide as low as 175 ppm, and it stayed under 400 ppm for 10 million years. Then the trend reversed. From a record low about 298 million years ago, carbon dioxide rose fourfold by 294 million years ago.

carb-042.title: Mountains bring monsoon rains
carb-042.text: The Central Pangean Mountains made their own weather. They set up a perennial monsoon over today's Europe and eastern North America, keeping those lands swampy while the Colorado Plateau stayed dry. Climate models suggest the range helped lay down vast coal deposits. The first signs of moisture moving toward the poles appeared in the late Carboniferous.

carb-043.title: The Cimmerian blocks break away
carb-043.text: A string of blocks that now lies in Asia began its journey from Gondwana. Rifting between India and the Cimmerian superterranes started in the Early Carboniferous, and the blocks pulled away in the Late Carboniferous. Stretching along Gondwana's northern margin set up their break-away and the opening of the Neo-Tethys in the early Permian. They would dock with Asia in the Triassic and Jurassic.

carb-044.title: Coal forests cover the tropics
carb-044.text:
About 90% of all coal beds formed in the Carboniferous and Permian, just 2% of Earth's history. The source was a world of swamps.

Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land in the Pennsylvanian and lasted into the Permian. Towering lycopsid rainforests dominated equatorial Euramerica, the high point of Paleozoic land plants, and peat mires also ringed the North and South China cratons. When the trees died, they piled up as peat, and the buried peat became coal.

The ice age helped. Glacial falls in sea level exposed wide shelves where peat mires grew, and rising seas in warmer spells then buried them. Why coal formation peaked so sharply is debated. One idea is a lag before fungi evolved that could digest lignin, the tough material in wood. The other is a unique mix of equatorial lands, high plant productivity and sinking wet basins.

carb-045.title: Cyclothems, stripes of a swinging sea
carb-045.text: The rocks of the Pennsylvanian repeat like a song. Cyclothems, repeating cycles of sediment, formed in shallow seas across tropical Laurussia and the China cratons. Each records a sea-level fall and rise over about 100,000 years, as Gondwana's ice sheets advanced and retreated on a Milankovitch cycle, a rhythm in Earth's orbit. The swings reached up to 120 m. Falls were slow and rises rapid, because ice sheets grow slowly but melt quickly.

carb-046.title: Equatorial Pangaea dries out
carb-046.text: The swamps did not last forever. Toward the end of the Carboniferous, Pangaea's equatorial belt grew drier, beginning a dry trend that lasted into the Triassic. After about 318 million years ago, seasons swung often between humid and arid, and a cycle of drying began in the late Moscovian, with abrupt changes in animal life. Late Pennsylvanian soils record drier, better-drained, more stable landscapes. Weaker weathering in the drier climate even lowered the seawater strontium-isotope ratio. Across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary, falling carbon dioxide and low-latitude aridity brought a permanent shift to seasonally dry woodland.

carb-047.title: Conifers and cycads appear
carb-047.text: Conifers began on dry ground. Early walchian conifers such as Walchia favored the higher, drier land where gymnosperms grew in the Pennsylvanian. The Voltziales conifers, cycads and Callistophytales seed ferns appeared in the late Carboniferous, and ginkgophytes also arose in the period. The oldest probable cycad leaves, such as Crossozamia from South Korea and China, date to around 300 million years ago.

carb-049.title: Arthropods grow to giant sizes
carb-049.text: Meganeura, a griffinfly, had wings spanning about 75 cm, the largest of any flying insect ever. It dominated the skies around 305 million years ago. On the ground crawled Arthropleura, a millipede-like animal up to 2.6 m long and the largest land invertebrate of all time. Arachnids, myriapods and especially flying insects underwent a major radiation in the late Carboniferous. Giant insects, millipedes and scorpions thrived while tetrapods stayed small, until {{ref:carb-071}}. The gigantism may reflect high oxygen levels, though how oxygen shaped body size is debated.

carb-051.title: The Oslo Rift tears open
carb-051.text: Around today's Oslo, the crust began to pull apart in the late Carboniferous, opening a graben, a block dropped between faults. The tearing came in the last phase of the Variscan orogeny and coincided with the Moscovian–Kasimovian boundary and the rainforest collapse. It ended in heavy volcanism: in Vestfold, rhomb porphyry lavas piled up about 3,000 m thick.

carb-052.title: The Ural Mountains begin to rise
carb-052.text: The Ural Mountains began rising about 323 million years ago. The Uralian orogeny started in the Late Carboniferous and went on through the Permian. Earlier, the Magnitogorsk island arc had collided with Baltica's margin from the Late Devonian to early Carboniferous. Then, as the Ural Ocean closed in the Bashkirian, Kazakhstania began colliding with Laurussia. Siberia, Kazakhstania and Baltica joined to form Laurasia, the basis of most of present-day Eurasia. Granites intruded the region as deformation continued, and around 300 million years ago the Urals were uplifted as Pangaea was finally sutured.

carb-053.title: Synapsids and sauropsids part ways
carb-053.text: Every mammal and every bird traces back to a single fork in the amniote family tree. Amniotes split into two lines: synapsids, the mammal lineage, and sauropsids, the line of reptiles and birds. Timelines place the first sauropsids around 320 million years ago and the first synapsids around 318 million years ago; the earliest fossils of both date to about 313 million years ago. Synapsid pelycosaurs appeared in the Late Carboniferous and went on to dominate land for some 40 million years. By the period's end, amniotes had diversified into pelycosaur families, protorothyridids, captorhinids, saurians and araeoscelids.

carb-057.title: Ice fills the young Karoo Basin
carb-057.text: Southern Africa lay inside the Antarctic Circle. Subduction under Gondwana and the rising Gondwanide mountains made room for a foreland basin, the Karoo Basin. Ice sheets buried the highlands around it, while floating glaciers filled its lowlands. Their deposits, tillites, diamictites and scratched rock pavements of the Dwyka Group, begin the Karoo Supergroup and reach about 800 m thick in the south.

carb-060.title: Hylonomus at Joggins, the oldest reptile
carb-060.text: The sea cliffs at Joggins, Nova Scotia, preserve a whole land ecosystem: lycopsid trees, giant arthropods and fish. They also yield Hylonomus, the oldest known sauropsid and one of the oldest reptiles in the fossil record. Here, in the coal-age forest, the reptile line makes its first clear appearance.

carb-062.title: The magnetic field stops flipping
carb-062.text: Earth's magnetic field normally reverses every so often. From about 312 to 262 million years ago, it did not. For more than 50 million years it held reversed polarity, with north and south swapped from today's arrangement. This stretch, the Kiaman superchron, spans the late Carboniferous to the late Permian. Comparable spells are the Cretaceous Normal Superchron and a possible one in the Ordovician.

carb-065.title: Mazon Creek's ironstone treasures
carb-065.text: The Tully monster, Tullimonstrum, is known from only one place: Mazon Creek, near Morris, Illinois. There a large delta preserved fossils in ironstone concretions in exceptional detail. Its roughly 200 insect species, some gigantic, show that insects already filled their main modern roles as plant eaters, scavengers of dead matter and insect eaters.

carb-067.title: A brief, intense Kasimovian glaciation
carb-067.text: Early in the Kasimovian, a glaciation lasting less than a million years drove carbon dioxide as low as 180 ppm. It was short but intense. It ended abruptly as carbon dioxide rose quickly, but by then the wetland forests had been restructured and the tree lycopsids lost.

carb-066.title: The Alykaevo Climatic Optimum
carb-066.text: Between the ice age's first and second major glacial periods came a warmer break. The Alykaevo Climatic Optimum, a relatively warm interglacial, spanned the Kasimovian and Gzhelian before the ice returned.

carb-071.title: The Carboniferous rainforest collapse
carb-071.text:
The great coal forests did not die out all at once; they broke into pieces. A cooler, drier climate first fragmented the rainforests and then collapsed them. Tree lycopsids and other wetland groups were lost in the Kasimovian glacial interval, as {{ref:carb-067}} describes.

It was a replacement more than an ending. Lycopsid forests gave way to tree-fern forests, a complex change, not the loss of all rainforest. Scale trees largely vanished from North America and Europe but persisted in Cathaysia, where coal forests even revived at the very end of the period.

Animals felt it too. Amphibians and amniotes were both hit, and the collapse may have let amniotes overtake amphibians, and seed plants overtake ferns and lycophytes. It was a minor extinction on land and at sea. But it left vast deserts across the continental interior, the landscape of the Permian to come.

carb-072.title: The first diapsid reptiles
carb-072.text: Petrolacosaurus, around 305 million years old, is among the first diapsid reptiles, the group with two openings behind each eye. By the end of the Carboniferous, amniotes included saurians and araeoscelids among several new groups. The reptile family tree was branching fast.

carb-074.title: The Ancestral Rocky Mountains
carb-074.text: Long before today's Rockies, another range stood in the same region. Around 300 million years ago, mountain building raised the Ancestral Rocky Mountains in what are now Colorado and New Mexico, with a prong into Wyoming. The Colorado orogeny that built them also began the Denver Basin. The range later eroded away.

carb-075.title: Hamilton Quarry's mixed fossils
carb-075.text: In Kansas, a probable estuary, where a river met the sea, mixed fossils from many settings. Hamilton Quarry preserves well-kept marine, brackish, freshwater, flying and land animals and plants side by side.

carb-076.title: The ice age peaks
carb-076.text: Around 300 million years ago, a very large part of Gondwana lay under glacial conditions. This exceptionally intense cooling marked the peak of the ice age across the Carboniferous–Permian boundary. A second major glacial period began in the late Gzhelian, with ice sheets spreading from cores in Australia and India into the early Permian. In the glacial maximum, 299–293 million years ago, the global average temperature was about 13 °C. Not everywhere froze at once. Brazil's Paraná Basin had its last glaciation in the early Gzhelian.

carb-077.title: Montceau-les-Mines fossil site
carb-077.text: Montceau-les-Mines, in France, preserves late Carboniferous life in exceptional detail, much like Mazon Creek. Its finds include vertebrates, arthropods and plants, among them temnospondyls, velvet worms and arachnids.

openers.pennsylvanian-subperiod: The Pennsylvanian was the age of coal. Vast freshwater swamp forests covered much of the tropical land, and oxygen climbed to 25–30%, above today's 21%, while carbon dioxide crashed to one of its lowest levels ever. Ice sheets spread from southern Africa and South America, and repeating rock cycles called cyclothems record the seas rising and falling with them. Arachnids, myriapods and flying insects radiated, cycads and conifers appeared, and by the end the equatorial belt was drying out.

reviews.pennsylvanian-subperiod: The Pennsylvanian's coal forests, air and ice were tied together. The forests buried carbon as peat, lifting oxygen to its highest level and helping drive carbon dioxide so low that ice sheets spread across Gondwana, while sea level rose and fell in cyclothems. Giant arthropods such as Meganeura and Arthropleura thrived in that air until a cooler, drier climate collapsed the rainforests. The collapse favored amniotes, which had split into synapsids and sauropsids, and seed plants such as conifers, while the Urals rose and Pangaea was sutured.
